opus-5.5.text:
Well, there are a couple of ways to go about it, and the nice thing is that you don't have to prove it from scratch. You can piggyback on results people have already established.

The most direct route is a reduction. Tensor logic has essentially one construct, the tensor equation: a join, which is an Einstein summation over shared indices, followed by a projection and optionally an elementwise nonlinearity. If you can show that some system already known to be universal can be written in that form, you're done. The obvious candidate is recurrent neural networks. Siegelmann and Sontag showed back in the nineties that RNNs are Turing complete, given the right conditions. An RNN is just a weight tensor multiplied by a state vector, passed through a nonlinearity and fed back into itself. That's a single tensor equation with recursion, so tensor logic can express any RNN, and therefore it inherits their universality.

You can also come at it from the logic side, which I find more illuminating. A Datalog rule is a tensor equation over Boolean tensors: the join of the relations in the body, projected onto the variables in the head, then a step function to bring it back to zero or one. Plain Datalog isn't Turing complete, because it always terminates on a finite domain. But once you allow unbounded domains, or the equivalent of function symbols, you get the expressive power of logic programming in general, and Prolog is universal. You could also simulate a Turing machine directly. You represent the tape, the head position and the machine state as tensors indexed by time step and position, and the transition function becomes a set of tensor equations that compute the configuration at t+1 from the configuration at t. Each step is a join and a projection. That's a very concrete, hands-on construction.

I want to add a caveat, though, because people sometimes make too much of Turing completeness. Lots of things are Turing complete, including some card games. Universality is a sanity check. It tells you there's nothing you fundamentally can't express. What I actually care about is whether the things we want to express are natural and compact in the language, and whether learning and reasoning are efficient. The real argument for tensor logic is that symbolic AI and neural networks turn out to be the same construct written in two notations. Universality is the minimum bar. The interesting part is what you can say easily once you've cleared it.

r001.rationale: The response proposes directly simulating a Turing machine by representing its tape, head position, and machine state, then encoding each transition as tensor equations. A Turing machine supplies finite control operating on a tape.

r002.rationale: The response proposes encoding recurrent neural networks as tensor equations and cites their established Turing completeness; it also gives logic-programming systems as another route.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the nice thing is you don't have to establish it from scratch. Tensor logic is basically one construct: a tensor equation, which is a Datalog rule where the atoms are tensors and the join is an Einstein summation. So the question reduces to showing that this one construct can express the things we already know are universal.

The most direct route is through logic programming. Datalog with function symbols, which is Prolog, is Turing complete. Tensor logic rules in the Boolean case are exactly Datalog rules, where the tensor entries are zero or one, the product of tensors along the shared indices is the conjunction, and summing out the unused indices followed by a step function is the existential quantifier. So anything you can write as a logic program, you can write as a set of tensor equations. Recursion is just a rule whose head appears in its own body, and you iterate to a fixed point. Once you have that, you have Turing completeness essentially for free, because you can encode a Turing machine's transition function as a relation and its tape as a tensor indexed by position, and the rule that computes the next configuration is a tensor equation.

The other route, which is maybe more interesting for this audience, goes through neural networks. A multilayer perceptron is a tensor equation: multiply the input by the weights, sum over the hidden index, apply a nonlinearity. Transformers are the same thing with a few more indices. And we know these are universal function approximators, and with recurrence they're Turing complete as well. So you get universality from both the symbolic side and the connectionist side, and the point of tensor logic is that it's the same object in both cases. The symbolic programs are the case where the tensors are Boolean and sparse, the neural networks are the case where they're real valued and dense, and everything in between, which is where reasoning in embedding space lives, is also expressible.

So if I were writing it down formally, I'd do the reduction from Datalog with function symbols, because that's a two-paragraph proof. But the thing I'd actually want people to take away is that you don't need Python wrapped around PyTorch anymore. The language and the model are the same thing.

r002.rationale: It proposes reducing the proof to Datalog with function symbols, described as Turing complete, and translating its logic programs into tensor equations.

astra-6.text:
The way to establish that is to show that TensorLogic can simulate a universal model of computation—for example, a Turing machine. You encode the machine’s state, tape contents, and head position as tensors, and express its transition rules as tensor operations. Then you show that iterating those operations reproduces the machine’s computation, step by step.

The important qualification is that you need iteration and arbitrarily extensible memory. A fixed tensor expression over fixed-size tensors doesn’t, by itself, establish Turing completeness. The universality claim is about the language with those capabilities, and the proof is an explicit encoding of a universal machine.

r001.rationale: It proposes simulating a Turing machine by encoding its state, tape contents, and head position, and says the memory must be arbitrarily extensible.

r002.rationale: It proposes encoding the transition rules of a known universal model, explicitly giving a Turing machine as an example.

sol-6.1.text:
The cleanest way is to show that it can simulate a Turing machine. You encode the tape symbols, the head position, and the machine’s state as predicates—or, equivalently, as entries in tensors—and then express the transition function as rules. Applying those rules repeatedly simulates successive steps of the machine.

The important qualification is that you need unbounded memory and iteration. A fixed-size tensor computation with a fixed number of steps isn’t computationally universal just because it can represent Boolean gates. You have to show that the representation can grow as needed and that the rules can keep executing. Once you establish those properties and give the simulation, you have a universality proof.

r001.rationale: It proposes simulating a Turing machine by encoding its tape symbols, head position, and state, and notes that the representation must support unbounded memory and iteration.

r002.rationale: It proposes expressing a Turing machine’s transition function as rules and applying them repeatedly; this encodes the rules of a known universal computational system in TensorLogic.
